source_text:
Ὅν τινες ἀγνοοῦντες ἀρνοῦνται, μᾶλλον δὲ ἠρνήθησαν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ, ὄντες συνήγοροι τοῦ θανάτου μᾶλλον ἢ τῆς ἀληθείας: οὓς οὐκ ἔπεισαν αἱ προφητεῖαι οὐδὲ ὁ νόμος Μωύσεως, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ μέχρι νῦν τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, οὐδὲ τὰ ἡμέτερα τῶν κατ’ ἄνδρα παθήματα.
καὶ γὰρ περὶ ἡμῶν τὸ αὐτὸ φρονοῦσιν. τί γάρ με ὠφελεῖ τις, εἰ ἐμὲ ἐπαινεῖ, τὸν δὲ κύριόν μου βλασφημεῖ, μὴ ὁμολογῶν αὐτὸν σαρκοφόρον; ὁ δὲ τοῦτο λέγων τελείως αὐτὸν ἀπήρνηται, ὢν νεκροφόρος.
τὰ δὲ ὀνόματα αὐτῶν, ὄντα ἄπιστα, οὐκ ἔδοξέν μοι ἐγγράψαι. ἀλλὰ μηδὲ γένοιτό μοι αὐτῶν μνημονεύειν, μέχρις οὗ μετανοήσωσιν εἰς τὸ πάθος, ὅ ἐστιν ἡμῶν ἀνάστασις.
thought_title: Deniers of Christ's flesh carry a corpse
orientation: Ignatius is warning the Smyrnaeans against teachers who deny that Christ truly suffered and rose in the flesh, and he now describes their denial and his refusal even to name them.
pass_a_gloss: Whom some, not knowing, deny, but rather they were denied by him, being advocates of death rather than of the truth; whom the prophecies did not persuade, nor the law of Moses, but not even until now the gospel, nor our own individual sufferings. For also about us they think the same thing. For what does someone benefit me, if he praises me, but blasphemes my Lord, not confessing him to be flesh-bearing? But the one saying this has completely denied him, being death-bearing. But their names, being faithless, it did not seem good to me to write down. But may it not even happen to me to remember them, until they repent into the passion, which is our resurrection.

choices.why: The compound adjective is central to Ignatius's anti-docetic point: Christ truly bore flesh. A literal rendering preserves the compound force and the contrast with νεκροφόρος.
The word is a coined compound paralleling σαρκοφόρον; rendering it literally keeps the sharp antithesis: the denier carries a corpse instead of confessing the flesh-bearing Lord.
συνήγορος is a legal term for an advocate or defense speaker; keeping 'advocates' preserves the courtroom force of the contrast with truth.

choices.term: τὰ ἡμέτερα τῶν κατ’ ἄνδρα παθήματα
choices.why: The phrase is awkward in Greek; the literal rendering keeps the possessive and the distributive force (sufferings man by man), which matters because Ignatius points to the martyrs as evidence.
The participle is predicative and continues the present-tense force of the denial; 'being' keeps the state described as ongoing.

pass_b_english: Some people deny him because they do not know him. Or rather, they have been denied by him, because they are advocates of death rather than of the truth. The prophecies did not persuade them, nor did the law of Moses, nor even to this day the gospel, nor our own individual sufferings.

For they think the same way about us as well. What good does it do me if someone praises me but blasphemes my Lord by refusing to confess that he bore flesh? The one who says this has completely denied him and is a bearer of death.
I did not think it right to write down their names, since they are faithless. But may I never even remember them until they repent concerning the passion, which is our resurrection.

problems.why: νεκροφόρος means 'death-bearing', not 'corpse-bearer'; cf. antithesis with σαρκοφόρον.
problems.ruling: νεκροφόρος means death-bearing, forming antithesis with σαρκοφόρον (flesh-bearing); corpse-bearer changes the meaning.

fixed: Changed 'corpse-bearer' to 'death-bearing' in both the English and the literal gloss, matching νεκροφόρος and preserving the antithesis with 'flesh-bearing'.

problems.why: Coinage; opposite of 'flesh-bearing' or 'life-bearing'; awkward but possibly original.
problems.fix: Accept as Ignatian coinage or check if 'death-dealing' better.

edits.new: and is a bearer of death.

fixed: The English 'death-bearing' was flagged as a coinage; replaced with 'a bearer of death' to convey the same meaning more naturally while preserving the contrast with 'flesh-bearing'.

last_rejected.why: Glossary fixes 'passion' for πάθος; 'death-bearing' misrenders νεκροφόρος.
last_rejected.ruling: νεκροφόρος literally means death-bearing/corpse-bearing; rendering is accurate and within normal range.

last_rejected.why: Greek says 'has completely denied him,' but context shows 'him' refers to Christ, not the speaker's Lord as in prior clause.
last_rejected.ruling: αὐτὸν refers to Christ throughout; 'him' correctly continues reference from 'my Lord' in preceding clause.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening contrast, replaced the awkward coinage 'flesh-bearing' with natural English 'bore flesh,' and made the final sentence flow more smoothly while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.why: Coinage; opposite of 'flesh-bearing' or 'life-bearing'; awkward but possibly original.
notes.fix: Accept as Ignatian coinage or check if 'death-dealing' better.
